t: Rectangle, freeform or kidney? Picking a shape
d: How shape changes the way you swim, lounge and landscape.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Rectangles give the most usable swimming length and suit modern homes.
  • Freeform curves feel like a resort and blend with natural stone and palms.
  • Kidney and plunge shapes suit lanai corners and townhome lots.

Shape is mostly about how you'll use the water and what your house looks like.

Who should choose a rectangular pool?

Clean lines suit modern and transitional homes. They also give the most usable swimming length, so they're great for laps. Try the Aussie, Bondi or Whitsunday.

Who should choose a freeform pool?

Curves feel like a resort and blend with palms and natural stone. Try Coral Sea or Billabong Cove.

Who should choose a kidney or plunge pool?

Soft, classic and compact. Kidney shapes wrap nicely around a lanai corner, and plunge pools fit townhome lots. Try Opal or Milano.

Not sure? Take the 30-second pool finder on our homepage, or drop any model into the 3D studio and walk around it.

t: Permits, HOAs and Florida pool safety rules
d: Who issues your pool permit in Duval, St. Johns and Clay counties, what HOAs ask for, and the safety feature Florida law requires.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Every inground pool in Northeast Florida needs a building permit. Under Florida law a spa or hot tub deeper than 24 inches counts as a pool too.
  • Who issues it depends on where you live: the City of Jacksonville, one of the beach cities, St. Johns County or Clay County.
  • To pass final inspection, a new residential pool needs at least one of five safety features set out in Chapter 515, Florida Statutes.
  • Most neighborhoods also need HOA approval. iTop prepares the drawings and handles both.

Every inground pool in Northeast Florida needs a building permit, and most neighborhoods also need HOA approval before anyone digs. iTop prepares the drawings, submits them and tracks each approval.

Do I need a building permit for a pool?

Yes. Your city or county reviews the site plan, setbacks, electrical and drainage before work starts, then inspects during the build and at the end. Florida's pool safety law defines a residential swimming pool as anything holding water over 24 inches deep, including hot tubs and nonportable spas, so a spa added to a pool is covered as well.

Who issues the permit where I live?

It depends on which government your address falls under, not your mailing city.

Where you liveWho issues the permitGood to know
Jacksonville (most of Duval County, including Mandarin)City of Jacksonville Building Inspection DivisionPermits are submitted online through JaxEPICS. Each pool or spa needs its own building permit, and the city asks for a signed Swimming Pool Safety Affirmation.
Jacksonville Beach, Atlantic Beach, Neptune BeachThat city's own building departmentThese beach cities run their own permitting, separate from the City of Jacksonville.
Unincorporated St. Johns County (Ponte Vedra Beach, St. Johns, Julington Creek, most of Nocatee)St. Johns County Building Department, 4040 Lewis Speedway, St. AugustineThe City of St. Augustine and St. Augustine Beach have their own building departments.
Unincorporated Clay County (Fleming Island, Middleburg)Clay County Building Division, Green Cove SpringsApplications go through the county's online Citizens Access Portal. The Town of Orange Park has its own building division.

Not sure which applies to you? Your property tax record shows your jurisdiction, and we check it before we draw anything.

Will my HOA need to approve it?

Many communities, including Nocatee, Julington Creek and Ponte Vedra neighborhoods, want drawings, materials and sometimes colors before approving. Some also set rules for fences, screen enclosures and equipment placement. Our 3D design and site plan give the review board what it needs in one package.

What does Florida's pool safety law require?

Florida's Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act (Chapter 515, Florida Statutes) says a new residential pool must have at least one of these to pass final inspection:

  1. A pool barrier that separates the pool from the house and meets the barrier rules in section 515.29 (height, gaps, and self-closing, self-latching gates).
  2. An approved safety pool cover.
  3. Exit alarms on every door and window that opens directly to the pool, rated at least 85 decibels at 10 feet.
  4. Self-closing, self-latching devices on every door that opens directly to the pool, with the release no lower than 54 inches above the floor.
  5. A pool alarm certified to ASTM F2208 that sounds when someone enters the water. Alarms worn by a child don't count.

Leaving out the safety feature is a second-degree misdemeanor under the same law, so it's settled before the final inspection, not after.

We'll recommend the safety option that fits your family and your yard, and build it into your quote. Many families combine more than one, such as door alarms plus a screen enclosure with a self-closing door.

What paperwork will I sign?

Expect an owner authorization for the permit, the pool safety affirmation where your jurisdiction uses one, and a Notice of Commencement, which Florida requires for most construction jobs of this size. We prepare them and tell you exactly where to sign.

Sources: Fla. Stat. §515.27 (safety features), §515.25 (definitions), City of Jacksonville Building Inspection Division, St. Johns County Building Department, Clay County Building Division. Requirements change and vary by jurisdiction; your permit reviewer has the final word.

t: How to choose a finish color
d: Why the same shell looks different in your yard, and how to pick with confidence.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Barrier Reef's US range has seven finishes.
  • Light finishes give turquoise water, and dark finishes look deeper and more reflective.
  • Depth, shade and deck color all change how the water looks.

Barrier Reef's US range has seven finishes: Aquamarine, Arctic, California, Evening Sky, Ocean, Sandstone and Silver Mist.

Should I choose a light or dark finish?

Light finishes such as Arctic and Sandstone give turquoise, Caribbean-style water. Dark finishes such as Ocean and Evening Sky look deeper and more reflective, like a lake.

What changes the color of the water?

  • Depth. The deep end always reads darker than the steps.
  • Sky and shade. A screen enclosure softens and darkens the water slightly.
  • Deck. Light travertine makes water look brighter. Charcoal pavers make it look moodier.
Compare any two finishes side by side in our color lab, then ask us to bring real samples to your site visit.

t: Tanning ledges, spas and lighting: what's worth it?
d: The upgrades owners use every week, and the ones they forget.
b:
Key takeaways
  • A tanning ledge is one of the upgrades owners use most.
  • Heat pumps suit Florida's mild winters and stretch the swim season.
  • Lighting and automation are cheap during the build and awkward to add later.

Some upgrades get used every day. Others get forgotten. Here's what we see owners use most.

Is a tanning ledge worth it?

A shallow shelf, usually under a foot of water. It's where chairs, toddlers and morning coffee end up. Highly recommended.

Should I add a spa?

Choose a shell with an integrated spa, like Sydney Harbour, or add a raised spillover spa. Great for cooler months.

Do I need a heat pump?

Florida's mild winters suit heat pumps well, and they stretch your swim season.

Are LED lighting and automation worth it?

Color LEDs and phone control for pump, lights and heat. Cheap to add during the build and awkward to add later.

Toggle a spa and tanning ledge in the 3D studio to see the difference, then price them in the estimator.

d: What happens from permit approval to the first swim.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Barrier Reef puts a typical install at 2–6 weeks once permits and HOA approval are in hand.
  • The shell arrives in one piece and is backfilled evenly while the pool fills.
  • Weather, inspections and enclosure lead times can change the timeline.

Once permits and HOA approval are in hand, a fiberglass install moves quickly. Barrier Reef puts a typical install at 2 to 6 weeks.

  1. Layout & locates. We mark the pool and call Sunshine 811 so utilities are located.
  2. Excavation. Usually a day or two, with soil hauled away.
  3. Delivery & set. The shell arrives in one piece and is lowered, leveled and plumbed.
  4. Backfill. We backfill evenly while the pool fills with water, to keep pressure balanced.
  5. Coping, deck & enclosure. The same crew lays the deck.
  6. Inspections. Final electrical and safety-feature inspections.
  7. Start-up & handover. We balance the water and show you how everything works.

Timeline varies with weather, inspections, site conditions and screen-enclosure lead times.

t: Site access: how a shell gets into your yard
d: Side gates, fences, cranes and what we check on the site visit.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Shells arrive on a truck in one piece, so the route into your yard matters.
  • Many pools can be set from the side, and fence panels can be removed and replaced.
  • Narrow lots or pools behind the house may need a crane.

Fiberglass shells arrive on a truck in one piece, so the route into your yard matters.

Can the shell come through my side yard?

If there's a clear path wide enough for equipment, we can usually set the shell from the side. Fence panels can be removed temporarily and replaced.

When is a crane needed?

Pools behind the house, narrow lots or screened areas may need a crane to lift the shell over. It's common, quick, and priced into your quote up front.

What do we check on the site visit?

  • Gate and side-yard widths
  • Overhead lines and trees
  • Septic, irrigation and drainage
  • Slope and soil

t: Your first 30 days as a pool owner
d: Start-up, chemistry basics and a simple weekly routine.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Run the pump as instructed and brush the walls and floor in week one.
  • Typical targets are pH 7.4–7.6, free chlorine 1–3 ppm and alkalinity 80–120 ppm.
  • A weekly routine takes about 10 minutes.

We'll start your pool and walk you through everything, but here's what to expect.

What happens in week one?

Run the pump as instructed, brush the walls and floor, and keep children's toys out until the water is balanced.

What should my water levels be?

  • pH: about 7.4–7.6
  • Free chlorine: about 1–3 ppm
  • Total alkalinity: about 80–120 ppm

Your handover sheet lists the exact targets for your pool and equipment. Saltwater systems still produce chlorine, so test just the same.

What is the weekly routine?

Skim, empty baskets, test, adjust, and give the floor a quick brush. The smooth gelcoat makes this the easy part.

d: What to do (and what never to do) before a storm.
b:
Key takeaways
  • Never drain a fiberglass pool, because high groundwater can push an empty shell up.
  • Don't restart equipment until it's dry and debris is cleared.
  • Call iTop after the storm if anything looks off.

Northeast Florida storms are part of life. Here's how to prepare your pool.

Do

  • Keep the pool full. The water's weight helps hold the shell in place.
  • Turn off pump, heater and lights at the breaker.
  • Bring in furniture, toys and loose décor.
  • Raise chlorine slightly before the storm.

Don't

  • Never drain a fiberglass pool. High groundwater after heavy rain can push an empty shell up.
  • Don't restart equipment until it's dry and debris is cleared.
After the storm, call us if anything looks off. We'd rather check than have you guess.
